newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Caspian oil explorers play down Turkmen tantrums.
newsitem.headline: Caspian oil explorers play down Turkmen tantrums.

text.p: Turkmenistan's territorial tantrums over who owns which energy reserves in the Caspian Sea are a cause for concern but should not affect existing deals, oil and gas executives said on Monday.

A $1 billion preliminary deal initialled on Friday between Azeri state oil company SOCAR and Russia's LUKoil and Rosneft to develop the Kyapaz oil field invoked the wrath of Ashgabat, which in a statement on Saturday claimed the field as its own.
Russian participants played down the row.

"It is obvious that the participants in the signing of the deal understand that the latent problem of the Caspian status exists," said Rosneft spokesman Vladimir Tumarkin. "But I don't think it will affect the fundamental aspects of our agreement."

Azeri President Haydar Aliyev presided over the signing of the deal during a visit to Moscow last week. The Kyapaz field, which Baku claims lies in its sector of the Caspian, is estimated to contain oil reserves of over 50 million tonnes.

LUKoil LKOH.RTS, Russia's biggest oil company and already a major force in the great Caspian oil game, said defining the Caspian's status and dividing it between littoral states was a matter for governments rather than oil companies.
"We have the right to sign deals with commercial structures -- in this case the Azeri state oil company," said Pyotr Neyev, LUKoil spokesman.
"But LUKoil won't take part in or comment on questions concerning territorial claims in the Caspian."
Countries bordering the Caspian have rowed for years over the status of the body of water and how it should be divided among them.

At stake are billions of dollars worth of oil and gas lying under the salty body of water, possibly the world's greatest untapped energy source and a prime target for the world's biggest oil companies.

Russia and Iran officially say the Caspian is a lake whose resources must be jointly exploited, while Turkmenistan, Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan insist it is a sea and that they are free to develop their sectors according to international law.
The puzzle is further muddled by claims by Turkmenistan to some fields Azerbaijan says lie in its sector of the Caspian.
The fact that Russian oil firms LUKoil and Rosneft have signed deals with Azerbaijan also points to a silent acceptance in Moscow of Baku's interpretation of the Caspian.

Turkmenistan used its protest over the Kyapaz field, which Ashgabat calls Serdar, to repeat claims to part or all of two other, much larger Caspian oil deposits under development by SOCAR and its foreign partners.

"Turkmenistan objects to the ignorance of its legal rights to the 'Kaverochkin' and '26 Baku commissars' fields, renamed 'Chirag' and 'Azeri' by Azerbaijan, which belong partially to Turkmenistan in the first case and fully in the second," the statement said.
The Chirag and Azeri fields, along with Gunashli, are under development by the huge $8 billion Azerbaijan International Operating Co (AIOC), which plans to start output in August.
But AIOC, led by the British Petroleum -Statoil alliance, said it was confident that spats over status would not hamper progress of the deal, Azerbaijan's biggest yet.
"AIOC management have said repeatedly that they are not concerned at all about negotiations on determining the status of the Caspian," said AIOC spokeswoman Tamam Bayatly in Baku.

AIOC did not have separate reserve estimates for the fields, but reserves of recoverable energy in the contract area containing the three fields are pegged at a massive 550 million tonnes of oil and 82 billion cubic feet of natural gas.
